topics.label: Introduction to cancer causes and lecture objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic frames the lecture by introducing the lecturer, situating the lecture in the course, and stating its aims.

topics.label: Cancer as mutation-driven clonal evolution shaped by host and microenvironment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain cancer as the accumulation of mutations and clonal advantages within a permissive microenvironment, shaped by endogenous, environmental, inherited, and cellular factors.

topics.label: Attributing cancer to environmental exposures versus bad luck
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics use examples of known and suspected exposures and the bad-luck debate to frame how environmental contributions to cancer should be understood.

topics.label: Geographical cancer patterns as evidence of environmental and genetic influences
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic compares cancer rates across regions and migration patterns to explore how environmental and inherited factors may shape incidence.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer development, including Burkitt lymphoma
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how pathogens can contribute to cancer, then develop Burkitt lymphoma as an example involving EBV, malaria, and MYC translocation.

topics.label: Mechanisms of DNA damage from environmental carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how particular environmental exposures produce DNA damage or mutational risk, including through metabolic activation.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain the distinction between mutational initiation and promotional conditions that support tumour growth.

topics.label: Developmental and tissue-specific susceptibility to carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics focus on how life stage and tissue context affect susceptibility to carcinogens, with the final subtopic summarizing context-dependent mechanisms.

topics.label: Identifying carcinogen exposure and its links to cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how human cancer and exposure data can be used to infer which carcinogens may have contributed to disease.

topics.label: Animal testing for carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic describes animal studies used to assess carcinogenicity and explains their limitations in predicting human risk.

topics.label: The Ames test for mutagenicity
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how the Ames test detects mutagenic activity and why the assay cannot capture all factors involved in cancer development.

topics.label: Risk–benefit decisions and lecture summary
topics.groupedBecause: This closing subtopic recaps the lecture’s conclusions and frames exposure to carcinogens as a matter of weighing risks and benefits.
